To answer your questions:
1) you dampen the compression to keep the fork from using all its travel when it's being compressed. Air pressure is how much force it takes to support you while allowing for the recommended sag. It's similar to a car spring—too weak and the vehicle will scrape the ground and bounce, and too stiff and the vehicle will be high and ride uncomfortably.

2) you have a lower-end shock, which likely only has adjustments for air pressure and rebound damping.

3) if you're bottoming out with the correct sag, then yes, you need to reduce the air chamber with spacers to achieve a sharper ramp up. However, too many volume spacers will make the fork too stiff and feel unpleasant.

You can add all the air you want, but if the compression circuit isn't damped well you'll still blow through travel. You won't bottom out the fork, but on braking the fork will dive easily and then get really stiff as it gets deeper into the travel. A good fork has controlled diving and has good mid travel support so that it doesn't feel like it gets super stiff all of a sudden. It's not bad to ride with some compression on, but it can make the fork harsh if you put on too much damping.
